title: Immediate building occupancy after the design earthquake, at life-safety cost

concept.text: The proposed innovation is an ordinary multi-storey residential or office building that remains ready for occupancy after design-level earthquake shaking, needs no structural repair, and costs no more to construct than a comparable local building designed to current life-safety requirements. The target combines structural performance, protection of occupancy-critical nonstructural systems, and construction economics. NIST’s functional-recovery work grounds the whole-building objective; immediate occupancy, no structural repair, and cost parity are the particular requirements proposed here.

Conceptual synthesis: the building must control damage during shaking and avoid permanent deformation that would require structural repair. Returning close to plumb is only one part of that outcome: nonstructural systems needed for safe occupancy must also remain usable. Base isolation, rocking systems, post-tensioned self-centering systems, and shape-memory alloys are candidate approaches identified in the supplied research, rather than required ingredients. An adaptive device that changes stiffness or damping in real time is optional.

The proposed boundary is performance under earthquake shaking, with permanent ground movement excluded. Actual reoccupancy also depends on required lifelines, access, and occupancy decisions. A building can therefore demonstrate readiness for occupancy while external infrastructure still prevents people from returning. NIST explicitly treats building lifelines and community infrastructure as part of the broader recovery problem.

significance.text: NIST describes preservation of occupants’ lives as the principal objective of prescriptive seismic codes for most buildings, while timely reoccupancy and recovery of function are not specifically addressed. Achieving immediate occupancy at the same construction cost would change what ordinary housing and workplaces could deliver after an earthquake: protection against loss of use would become an affordable design outcome alongside life protection.

Conditional consequence: for buildings meeting the target, structural and occupancy-critical nonstructural damage would no longer force loss of use after the specified shaking. This could reduce displacement, business interruption, and repair-related downtime attributable to those buildings, provided required lifelines and access remained available. Construction-cost parity would remove one potential obstacle to broad adoption, but would not by itself establish equal lifetime costs or guarantee deployment.

The citywide impact would depend on widespread adoption, functioning utilities and transport, inspection and recovery arrangements, and the vulnerability of the remaining building stock. NIST’s recovery framework explicitly extends beyond individual structures to communities and community infrastructure. One successful new building would therefore demonstrate a valuable capability without establishing that a design-level earthquake could no longer disrupt a city.

Scope synthesis: extending the approach to existing nonductile buildings could be valuable, but retrofit performance and economics require separate demonstration. Nor does the proposed advance depend on proving that immediate-occupancy performance is currently confined to hospitals or landmarks; the distinguishing target is the complete combination of ordinary-building scope, occupancy readiness, and construction-cost parity.

missing_breakthrough.text: The capability to establish is an integrated building system that simultaneously avoids structural repair, protects occupancy-critical nonstructural systems, and meets the local construction-cost benchmark under a defined design earthquake. NIST supports the need to address structural systems, nonstructural systems, and lifelines together. The supplied evidence does not establish that this complete combination has been demonstrated, but it also does not establish that no qualifying demonstration exists.

Engineering synthesis: the central integration challenge is to dissipate earthquake energy while limiting both damaging deformation during shaking and permanent deformation afterward. A system that recenters can still leave damage requiring repair, and a structurally sound frame can still contain nonstructural damage that prevents occupancy. A convincing solution must therefore connect measured structural response to damage and usability across the whole building, rather than treating self-centering alone as sufficient.

Engineering synthesis: the practical breakthrough must also survive installation and construction constraints without shifting costs into foundations, connections, nonstructural protection, or specialized fabrication. The earlier research identifies material cost, temperature sensitivity, device size, and nonstructural drift as possible barriers. The supplied evidence does not establish their comparative importance across isolation, rocking, post-tensioned self-centering, and shape-memory-alloy systems, or justify a blanket claim that these technologies are kept out of ordinary buildings.

A further challenge is translating engineering performance into an assessable occupancy outcome. NIST explains that increasing structural design loads does not explicitly address building functionality or recovery time, and that common performance-based design metrics are not expressed in recovery time. This target therefore needs explicit links between damage, required repairs, system usability, and the decision to permit occupancy.

current_state.text: NIST’s project page, created on 15 October 2019 and updated on 26 March 2025 according to the supplied research, identifies the gap between life-preservation objectives and timely recovery. It recognizes that performance-based seismic design can target Immediate Occupancy, while explaining that common design metrics do not directly express recovery time. Its proposed functional-recovery approach addresses damage to the building and its contents, together with lifelines and community recovery needs. This documents an established engineering objective, rather than a demonstration of the complete performance-and-cost target.

SOM describes a network of tension rods incorporating shape-memory-alloy cables for UC Berkeley’s Grimes Engineering Center, intended to return toward its original position after deformation and improve seismic resilience. The firm characterizes the application as the first use of SMA technology in a building lateral force-resisting system in new construction. That narrower claim concerns the system and application, not every possible use of SMA in a new building. It is a designer-reported project claim, without independent verification of global priority or evidence here of immediate occupancy after design-level shaking.

The supplied review reports complete retained webpage text for SOM, but its embedded testing video and other visual material were not inspected. The project page supplies no comparative construction-cost evidence. Consequently, the reported application supports a relevant self-centering approach without establishing whole-building occupancy performance, absence of structural repair, or cost parity.

The earlier research attributes material-price comparisons to a review titled “Shape memory alloys application in civil infrastructure: A review of reinforcement, retrofitting and seismic resilience,” dated 1 December 2025: approximately 8–12 times the cost per mass of conventional reinforcement for NiTi alloys and 2–3 times for iron-based alloys. It also attributes a restriction to critical retrofits to that review. These remain unverified attributions: the supplied source index contains no captured text or artifact for the article, and the validated review could not confirm its identity, comparison basis, or deployment claim. The earlier research also records that the author list and full text were not opened and the journal title was not displayed. Even if verified, material prices per unit mass would not by themselves establish a whole-building construction-cost premium. Missing retained evidence does not show that the reported numbers are false.

Evidence boundary: the supplied record contains no freshness-search entries establishing whether the complete capability had been achieved by 1 November 2026. The dated NIST statements and qualified SOM project report remain useful, but they cannot support a definitive claim that the innovation is either achieved or still absent worldwide.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: construct a multi-storey residential or office building for no more than a comparable local code life-safety building of the same size. State the cost date, accounting boundary, site conditions, program, and equivalent comparison assumptions so that cost parity can be assessed. Include the systems needed to deliver the claimed occupancy outcome within that boundary. A flagship isolated hospital alone would not satisfy the ordinary-building scope. These are proposed criteria for this concept, not established standards.
completion_criteria.label: Ordinary multi-storey construction achieves fully accounted local life-safety cost parity

completion_criteria.text: Proposed performance test: use either a full-scale shake-table experiment or a recorded earthquake that meets a predefined design-level shaking criterion. Document the input motion, structural damage, residual drift, and condition of occupancy-critical nonstructural systems. Establish that the building requires no structural repair and that systems needed for occupancy remain usable without reconstruction. Define acceptable damage and residual deformation before assessing the result; a small residual drift measurement alone is insufficient.
completion_criteria.label: Design-level shaking leaves occupancy-critical systems usable without structural repair

completion_criteria.text: Proposed occupancy assessment: after a real earthquake, document the assessment permitting occupancy and actual reoccupancy. For a shake-table experiment, document an equivalent assessment of occupancy readiness, including the scope of systems represented in the test. Verify required lifelines and access, or explicitly state assumptions about them. These distinctions operationalize NIST’s whole-building recovery objective while keeping laboratory readiness separate from actual return to use.
completion_criteria.label: Post-shaking assessment establishes actual reoccupancy or laboratory occupancy readiness

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and boundaries: publish sufficient design, construction, cost, shaking, damage, and occupancy-assessment information for independent evaluation and replication. Further demonstrations should test the building types, heights, site conditions, and shaking characteristics for which applicability is claimed. State the exclusion of permanent ground movement and any untested retrofit application. Finite demonstrations establish performance over the tested range, not universal earthquake immunity. Passive systems can qualify; adaptive devices are not required.
completion_criteria.label: Published information enables independent replication and states applicability limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: CIV-12, “Fail-safe adaptive primary structural response at ordinary-building cost,” overlaps through structural response and affordability. CIV-12 concerns an adaptive structural capability; CIV-09 concerns the resulting whole-building occupancy outcome and construction cost. An adaptive system could contribute to CIV-09, but adaptation alone does not demonstrate nonstructural usability or occupancy readiness. Conversely, a passive system could satisfy CIV-09 without satisfying CIV-12.

Roster-based synthesis: CIV-02, “Mechanics-based prediction of earthquake liquefaction and its ground consequences,” addresses prediction of ground behavior, while CIV-03, “In-place conversion of ordinary ground into a specified engineering solid,” addresses modification of the ground. Both can matter to earthquake resilience, but neither is equivalent to maintaining building occupancy under shaking. CIV-09 explicitly excludes permanent ground movement. These distinctions follow from the supplied titles and stated boundary; fuller definitions of CIV-02 and CIV-03 were not supplied.

Roster-based synthesis: CIV-04, “Repeated recovery of structural load capacity after cracking,” overlaps with structural damage tolerance and recovery, while CIV-05, “Tensile-ductile mineral structures that replace reinforced concrete at ordinary cost,” could offer a material route toward affordable seismic performance. Recovering load capacity after cracking does not itself establish immediate occupancy without structural repair, and material ductility at ordinary cost does not establish whole-building performance. Both remain distinct from CIV-09’s combined structural, nonstructural, usability, and economic requirements.

change_log.reason: The review supports the coherence of the concept even though the supplied evidence does not resolve whether the full capability has already been demonstrated.

change_log.reason: The source record does not establish the worldwide state of the complete capability through 1 November 2026.

change_log.change: Integrated structural, nonstructural, lifeline, and occupancy requirements while distinguishing self-centering from whole-building usability.
change_log.reason: NIST supports an integrated recovery objective; returning a structure toward plumb alone does not establish occupancy.

change_log.change: Retained the reported SMA cost ratios as explicitly unverified attributions and qualified the claimed restriction to critical retrofits.
change_log.reason: The user requests preservation of quantitative detail and uncertainty. No article text was retained to verify the figures, their comparison basis, or the deployment assertion.

change_log.change: Narrowed SOM’s first-use attribution to SMA technology in a building lateral force-resisting system in new construction and retained its access limitations.
change_log.reason: That is the scope supported by the supplied review; the designer’s claim does not independently establish global priority, cost parity, or demonstrated occupancy performance.

change_log.change: Reframed citywide continuity and retrofit applicability as conditional downstream possibilities.
change_log.reason: Widespread deployment, external infrastructure, recovery arrangements, and separate retrofit validation are needed beyond one successful new-building demonstration.

change_log.reason: These details permit evaluation of the claimed combination while distinguishing laboratory occupancy readiness from actual reoccupancy.

change_log.reason: The roster permits bounded conceptual comparisons, while its titles do not establish detailed technical scope or demonstrated capabilities.

unresolved_issues: Whether any ordinary building has demonstrated the complete occupancy, no-structural-repair, and construction-cost-parity target remains unresolved by the supplied record.

The December 2025 SMA review’s identity, cost comparison basis, numerical ratios, and alleged restriction to critical retrofits require retained source evidence. The recommendation to remove the ratios was not followed literally because the user requests preserving unresolved quantitative detail; they are retained only as unverified attributions.
Comparative evidence is missing for the claimed cost, temperature, device-size, nonstructural-drift, and adoption barriers across the candidate structural approaches.

SOM’s global first-use attribution, whole-building earthquake performance, and comparative construction costs are not independently established here; embedded testing material was not inspected in the supplied review.
The proposal still needs project-specific definitions of design-level shaking, acceptable damage and residual drift, immediate-occupancy timing, cost accounting, and occupancy-assessment procedures.
The practical boundary between building occupancy readiness and actual reoccupancy depends on required lifelines, access, and inspection arrangements.
Detailed scope beyond the supplied roster titles, and applicability to existing nonductile buildings, remain to be established.

brief.title: Homes and workplaces ready to use after an earthquake
possible: People could return immediately to ordinary multi-storey homes and offices after the earthquake shaking they were designed to withstand. The buildings would need no structural repair, and the systems needed for safe occupancy would remain usable.
These buildings would cost no more to construct than comparable local buildings designed to protect lives under current requirements.
why: Most building codes focus on keeping people alive during an earthquake. Making continued use an affordable design goal would also protect residents from displacement and businesses from repair-related closures.

sources.who: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.showed: NIST describes a framework for returning buildings to use after earthquakes. It connects damage to the structure, internal systems and supporting utilities with recovery time.
sources.cited_for: Occupancy depends on the whole building and its supporting services, beyond whether the structure survives.
sources.not_established: The framework does not demonstrate an ordinary building that remains immediately usable without structural repair at equal construction cost.

sources.who: Authors of the review on shape-memory alloys in civil infrastructure
sources.showed: This is a review of shape-memory alloys, metals that regain their shape after deformation, for reinforcing buildings, upgrading existing structures and resisting earthquakes.
sources.cited_for: It concerns candidate materials for limiting earthquake damage.
sources.not_established: Material price comparisons alone cannot establish the construction cost of a complete building.

sources.who: Skidmore, Owings & Merrill and TriPyramid Structures
sources.showed: SOM developed rods incorporating shape-memory-alloy cables for UC Berkeley’s Grimes Engineering Center. It reports prototype testing and describes the system as helping control sideways roof movement during shaking.
sources.quote: The SMA material is composed into wire ropes reconciled into tension rods through connectors that were collaboratively developed with TriPyramid Structures.
sources.cited_for: A building project uses a system designed to return toward its original position after deformation.
sources.not_established: The project does not establish immediate occupancy after the specified shaking, freedom from structural repair or equal construction cost.

shown: SOM reports developing and testing prototype rods with shape-memory-alloy cables for UC Berkeley’s Grimes Engineering Center. The system aims to limit earthquake damage by returning toward its original shape. This is a designer-reported application; whole-building occupancy performance and comparative construction costs remain unestablished.
missing: An integrated demonstration must combine freedom from structural repair with usable systems for safe occupancy after the specified shaking.
A complete construction-cost comparison must include foundations, connections and all protection needed to keep the building usable.
An occupancy assessment must connect measured damage and system condition to permission to return or equivalent laboratory readiness.

milestones.label: An ordinary building matches local construction costs
milestones.explanation: A multi-storey home or office building would have to match a comparable local life-protection design’s construction cost, including all occupancy protections. Comparable accounting would establish affordability.

milestones.label: Specified shaking leaves the building usable without structural repair
milestones.explanation: A full-scale shaking test or recorded earthquake would have to meet predefined shaking and damage criteria, leaving occupancy systems usable without structural repair. This would test the whole building’s performance.

milestones.label: Assessment establishes return to use or laboratory readiness
milestones.explanation: Assessment would have to establish permitted and actual return after an earthquake, or equivalent laboratory readiness, with utility and access assumptions explicit. This would connect performance to occupancy.

milestones.label: Published results support independent replication and define limits
milestones.explanation: Published design, cost, shaking, damage and occupancy details would have to enable replication across claimed conditions. Defined limits would exclude permanent ground movement and identify untested upgrades to existing buildings.

uncertain: Whether any ordinary building already meets the complete performance and construction-cost target remains unresolved.
The shaking level, acceptable damage, timing of occupancy and cost comparison need project-specific definitions.
Actual return depends on utilities, access and inspection arrangements even when the building itself is ready.

page.title: Immediate occupancy at life-safety construction cost
page.definition: Multi-storey homes and offices remain safe to occupy immediately after local code design-earthquake shaking, without structural repair and at no greater construction cost than comparable code-minimum buildings. Their nonstructural systems—components such as stairs, fire protection and utilities—remain usable where needed for occupancy, assuming external services and access are available.

goal.need: FEMA and NIST cite estimates in which modern code-conforming buildings rendered unfit for occupancy require months or years of repair, while economically unrepairable buildings require many years for replacement. Preserving occupancy addresses disruption that protection against collapse alone does not prevent.

figures.caption: Estimated consequences for modern code-conforming buildings following a large earthquake.
figures.note: FEMA study estimates summarized in FEMA P-2090/NIST SP-1254; these are conditional estimates, not observed worldwide frequencies.

statements.body: National Institute of Standards and Technology
statements.quote: Initial costs are a primary driver of IO decisions for developers and building owners.

completion.title: Design shaking leaves a building immediately occupiable without structural repair or added construction cost.
completion.criterion: One completed multi-storey residential or office building demonstrates immediate safe occupancy after shaking meeting its local code's design-earthquake demand, with no required structural repair and all occupancy-critical systems usable. Total construction cost is no greater than a matched local code-minimum life-safety design, priced for the same date, site, floor area and programme, including foundations, connections and nonstructural protection. Evidence comprises full-scale testing or an instrumented earthquake and an occupancy-readiness assessment. Required lifelines and access are available; permanent ground displacement is excluded.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; no outside body was found to have published the combined performance-and-cost test.
completion.basis: Searched NIST recovery reports, FEMA performance levels, Arup's REDi FAQs and construction-cost studies for a joint occupancy/no-structural-repair/cost-parity test; none was found. FEMA 356 permits minor structural repairs at Immediate Occupancy. The conjunction and zero premium are Atlas criteria. For one four-storey concrete-frame office archetype, NIST estimated construction costs of $527/ft² for the baseline and $557/ft² with combined enhancements, using 2023 Los Angeles costs.

milestones.title: A building retains a margin against partial or total collapse after its specified earthquake shaking.
milestones.criterion: Meet FEMA 356 structural Life Safety level S-3 for the specified earthquake demand: damage may occur, but a margin against partial or total collapse remains and component acceptance criteria are satisfied. Between June and September 1999, one five-storey PRESSS concrete specimen at 60% scale sustained input at least 50% above UBC Zone 4 requirements, with minimal wall-direction damage and no significant frame-direction strength loss at drifts up to 4.5%. This is experimental evidence bearing on the damage-state criterion, not a FEMA certification.
milestones.set_by: FEMA, FEMA 356, Section 1.5.1.3; published in November 2000 for rehabilitation of existing buildings.
milestones.threshold_quote: retains a margin against onset of partial or total collapse

milestones.title: A building retains nearly all structural strength and stiffness after its specified earthquake shaking.
milestones.criterion: Meet FEMA 356 structural Immediate Occupancy level S-1: safe occupancy, essentially retained pre-earthquake strength and stiffness, and applicable component acceptance criteria. Minor structural repairs may be appropriate but need not precede reoccupancy. The 2024 TallWood paper reports one full-scale, 34 m, ten-storey timber specimen subjected to 88 earthquake tests, including maximum-considered motions, with no detected structural damage or observed residual drift. These observations support the damage-state objective; formal S-1 compliance was not established.
milestones.set_by: FEMA, FEMA 356, Sections 1.5.1.1 and C1.5.1.1; published in November 2000 for rehabilitation of existing buildings.
milestones.threshold_quote: retains the pre-earthquake design strength and stiffness of the structure

milestones.title: A building's access and life-safety systems remain operable after shaking, permitting immediate occupancy.
milestones.criterion: Meet FEMA 356 building Immediate Occupancy level 1-B at the specified earthquake demand: structural S-1 plus nonstructural N-B. Doors, stairs, elevators, emergency lighting, fire alarms and suppression systems generally remain available and operable if power is available; normal use may still be impaired. TallWood's partitions, façades and stairs remained safe and operational despite repairable damage. These are partial system results, not a demonstration of every system required for occupancy.
milestones.set_by: FEMA, FEMA 356, Sections 1.5.3.2, 1.5.2.2 and their commentary; published in November 2000 for rehabilitation of existing buildings.

not_found: No verified demonstration satisfying the combined completion test was found.
A complete assessment of every occupancy-critical system was not found for the TallWood specimen.
The supplied shape-memory-alloy review could not be opened; its attributed material-price ratios remain unverified.

results.finding: One full-scale six-story hybrid timber-steel specimen showed no story mechanisms under testing that included MCER shaking.
results.detail: The test included design-level and maximum considered earthquake shaking. The observed performance bears on collapse resistance, but the paper does not assess FEMA 356 S-3 component acceptance criteria or establish a collapse margin.
results.quote:
No story mechanisms were 
recorded during testing, with IDRs meeting ASCE 7-16
transient drift requirements.

results.finding: One elevator remained functional after design-event shaking with a 2.5% peak interstory drift ratio.
results.detail: The elevator had minor door and surrounding partition damage. The result covers one system and does not establish FEMA 356 S-1 plus N-B performance for the whole building. More severe subsequent shaking made the elevator inoperable.
results.quote: The elevator remained functioning up to and including the design event earthquake.
